chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: Preface In 1963 a plan was formulated at the Office of Population Research at Princeton University to document the decline in the rate of child¬ bearing in Europe, province by province.
text_raw:
Preface 
In 1963 a plan was formulated at the Office of Population Research 
at Princeton University to document the decline in the rate of child¬ 
bearing in Europe, province by province.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: In nearly every one of the more than seven hundred European provinces women today are bearing no more than half the number of children born a few generations ear¬ lier; however, the timing and the pace of this nearly universal decline in fertility differs widely from area to area.
text_raw:
In nearly every one of the 
more than seven hundred European provinces women today are bearing 
no more than half the number of children born a few generations ear¬ 
lier; however, the timing and the pace of this nearly universal decline 
in fertility differs widely from area to area.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: The principal purpose of the European Fertility Project is a better understanding of the circum¬ stances that have contributed to a lower rate of childbearing, cir¬ cumstances that may be of considerable interest for rapidly growing populations today.
text_raw:
The principal purpose of 
the European Fertility Project is a better understanding of the circum¬ 
stances that have contributed to a lower rate of childbearing, cir¬ 
cumstances that may be of considerable interest for rapidly growing 
populations today.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: An incidental purpose is to record and analyze a significant feature of the recent social history of every European popu¬ lation.
text_raw:
An incidental purpose is to record and analyze a 
significant feature of the recent social history of every European popu¬ 
lation.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: The project has taken the form of a series of country studies carried out at Princeton and by colleagues at other American universities and in Europe.
text_raw:
The project has taken the form of a series of country studies carried 
out at Princeton and by colleagues at other American universities and 
in Europe.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: The studies utilize the same set of fertility measures, and each aims to cover the period from the beginning of the modern de¬ cline to its end, or in some instances, to the present.
text_raw:
The studies utilize the same set of fertility measures, and 
each aims to cover the period from the beginning of the modern de¬ 
cline to its end, or in some instances, to the present.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: This is the sixth book to present results of research on the fertility of particular Euro¬ pean populations.
text_raw:
This is the sixth 
book to present results of research on the fertility of particular Euro¬ 
pean populations.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: The first five—A Century of Portuguese Fertility and A History of Italian Fertility during the Last Two Centuries by Mas¬ simo Livi-Bacci, The Decline of Fertility in Germany, 1871-1939 by John Knodel, The Decline of Belgian Fertility, 1800-1970 by Ron J.
text_raw:
The first five—A Century of Portuguese Fertility and 
A History of Italian Fertility during the Last Two Centuries by Mas¬ 
simo Livi-Bacci, The Decline of Fertility in Germany, 1871-1939 by 
John Knodel, The Decline of Belgian Fertility, 1800-1970 by Ron J.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: Lesthaeghe, and The Female Population of France in the Nineteenth Century by Etienne van de Walle—have dealt with geographic sub¬ divisions within countries in Southern or Western Europe.
text_raw:
Lesthaeghe, and The Female Population of France in the Nineteenth 
Century by Etienne van de Walle—have dealt with geographic sub¬ 
divisions within countries in Southern or Western Europe.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: Other stud¬ ies of Great Britain, Switzerland, Scandinavia, and a second volume on France are in process.
text_raw:
Other stud¬ 
ies of Great Britain, Switzerland, Scandinavia, and a second volume 
on France are in process.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: In addition to books and articles on national populations, a conference is planned (in 1979) at which there will be a summary presentation of province-by-province statistics for all of Europe and a series of papers dealing with particular features of Euro¬ pean fertility history, such as rural-urban differences, the geographical clustering of fertility patterns, and the relations to education and infant mortality.
text_raw:
In addition to books and articles on national 
populations, a conference is planned (in 1979) at which there will be 
a summary presentation of province-by-province statistics for all of 
Europe and a series of papers dealing with particular features of Euro¬ 
pean fertility history, such as rural-urban differences, the geographical 
clustering of fertility patterns, and the relations to education and infant 
mortality.

chapter_title: Chapter 5
text: HUMAN FERTILITY IN RUSSIA SINCE THE NINETEENTH CENTURY
text_raw:
HUMAN FERTILITY IN RUSSIA 
SINCE THE NINETEENTH CENTURY

chapter_title: Chapter 5
Chapter 1: Introduction
text: In the last two centuries, two widely occurring basic changes in the dynamics of population have profoundly modified the lifetime experience of individuals and the structure of the societies in which they live: a dramatic increase in the average duration of life; and a dramatic decrease in the average number of children women bear by the end of their po¬ tentially fertile years.
text_raw:
In the last two centuries, two widely occurring basic changes in the 
dynamics of population have profoundly modified the lifetime experience 
of individuals and the structure of the societies in which they live: a 
dramatic increase in the average duration of life; and a dramatic decrease 
in the average number of children women bear by the end of their po¬ 
tentially fertile years.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The mean length of life has increased as the risk of dying has been reduced at every age because of increases in real in¬ come and improvements in preventive and curative medicine; the num¬ ber of children born has declined as married couples have been success¬ ful in deliberate efforts to restrict childbearing.
text_raw:
The mean length of life has increased as the risk 
of dying has been reduced at every age because of increases in real in¬ 
come and improvements in preventive and curative medicine; the num¬ 
ber of children born has declined as married couples have been success¬ 
ful in deliberate efforts to restrict childbearing.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The decline in mortality has in many instances doubled the mean duration of life, and the de¬ cline in fertility has frequently reduced by one-half the number of chil¬ dren women bear.
text_raw:
The decline in mortality 
has in many instances doubled the mean duration of life, and the de¬ 
cline in fertility has frequently reduced by one-half the number of chil¬ 
dren women bear.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The decrease in mortality began in Western Europe in the late eight¬ eenth century with rather modest declines in death rates, and it has continued up to the present.
text_raw:
The decrease in mortality began in Western Europe in the late eight¬ 
eenth century with rather modest declines in death rates, and it has 
continued up to the present.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Once death rates began to fall in Latin America, Asia, and Africa (much later, often only within the past few decades), the reductions were frequently very large.
text_raw:
Once death rates began to fall in Latin 
America, Asia, and Africa (much later, often only within the past few 
decades), the reductions were frequently very large.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The fall in death rates has by now become so general that it has been shared by every national population in the world.
text_raw:
The fall in death 
rates has by now become so general that it has been shared by every 
national population in the world.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The decrease in fertility—the sustained modern decline that is associated with the spread of voluntary birth control—became evident on a national scale in France by the beginning of the nineteenth century, and perhaps began at about the same time in the United States.1 In Western European countries other than France, the decline began in the second half of the nineteenth century.
text_raw:
The decrease in fertility—the sustained 
modern decline that is associated with the spread of voluntary birth 
control—became evident on a national scale in France by the beginning 
of the nineteenth century, and perhaps began at about the same time 
in the United States.1 In Western European countries other than France, 
the decline began in the second half of the nineteenth century.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: It began later in Southern and Eastern Europe—in Albania, as late as the post- World War II period.
text_raw:
It began 
later in Southern and Eastern Europe—in Albania, as late as the post- 
World War II period.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Before 1910, large decreases in fertility had been initiated in most overseas areas populated by Europeans, including (in addition to the United States) Canada, Argentina, Australia, and New Zealand.
text_raw:
Before 1910, large decreases in fertility had been 
initiated in most overseas areas populated by Europeans, including (in 
addition to the United States) Canada, Argentina, Australia, and New 
Zealand.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: A very large fall has also occurred in Japan, although the date of its beginning is hard to determine from the available records.
text_raw:
A very large fall has also occurred in Japan, although the date 
of its beginning is hard to determine from the available records.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The decline in fertility has been a universal feature of the recent his¬ tory of all countries that are usually accepted as the most highly de¬ veloped, that is, those characterized by a fully modern organization of society and economic life.
text_raw:
The decline in fertility has been a universal feature of the recent his¬ 
tory of all countries that are usually accepted as the most highly de¬ 
veloped, that is, those characterized by a fully modern organization of 
society and economic life.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Fertility has also begun to fall, usually at a faster rate than was experienced by European populations, in many [3]
text_raw:
Fertility has also begun to fall, usually at a 
faster rate than was experienced by European populations, in many 
[3]

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: INTRODUCTION countries that are not so highly modernized.
text_raw:
INTRODUCTION 
countries that are not so highly modernized.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Unlike the decline in mor¬ tality, however, a reduction in fertility has not yet started in all na¬ tional populations.
text_raw:
Unlike the decline in mor¬ 
tality, however, a reduction in fertility has not yet started in all na¬ 
tional populations.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Little or no change is evident in some populations in Asia (none in Bangladesh, parts of India, and Afghanistan, for ex¬ ample), in Africa (for example, no change in virtually all of tropical Africa, nor in parts of north Africa), nor in Latin America (little change, for example, in Bolivia, Peru, and, until very recently at least, Mexico).
text_raw:
Little or no change is evident in some populations 
in Asia (none in Bangladesh, parts of India, and Afghanistan, for ex¬ 
ample), in Africa (for example, no change in virtually all of tropical 
Africa, nor in parts of north Africa), nor in Latin America (little 
change, for example, in Bolivia, Peru, and, until very recently at least, 
Mexico).

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Lower mortality has an obvious implication of great importance to the individual: longer life itself.
text_raw:
Lower mortality has an obvious implication of great importance to 
the individual: longer life itself.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Lower death rates also mean that siblings and friends survive rather than die at an early age.
text_raw:
Lower death rates also mean that 
siblings and friends survive rather than die at an early age.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: With pres¬ ent-day low mortality rates, a child usually reaches his adult years without experiencing the death of a brother, sister, or close friend, and frequently with both parents still alive—all outcomes of childhood life that would have been exceptional a few generations back.
text_raw:
With pres¬ 
ent-day low mortality rates, a child usually reaches his adult years 
without experiencing the death of a brother, sister, or close friend, and 
frequently with both parents still alive—all outcomes of childhood life 
that would have been exceptional a few generations back.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Parents now rarely lose children, and the early disruption of marriage by death of a spouse has become uncommon.
text_raw:
Parents now 
rarely lose children, and the early disruption of marriage by death of a 
spouse has become uncommon.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The forces that have reduced mortality have also brought reductions in chronic fever and other debilitating or painful consequences of infectious disease.
text_raw:
The forces that have reduced mortality 
have also brought reductions in chronic fever and other debilitating or 
painful consequences of infectious disease.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: To the individual child, lower fertility means that he grows up in the company of fewer siblings.
text_raw:
To the individual child, 
lower fertility means that he grows up in the company of fewer siblings.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: When low fertility is combined with low mortality, children more fre¬ quently have living parents and grandparents, but young adults have fewer children, and older adults fewer grandchildren.
text_raw:
When low fertility is combined with low mortality, children more fre¬ 
quently have living parents and grandparents, but young adults have 
fewer children, and older adults fewer grandchildren.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Reduced fertility and mortality affect society as a whole, first of all by increasing the rate of growth and altering the age structure of the population.
text_raw:
Reduced fertility and mortality affect society as a whole, first of all 
by increasing the rate of growth and altering the age structure of the 
population.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The decline in mortality, which often precedes the fall in fertility, has caused a truly exceptional increase in global population.
text_raw:
The decline in mortality, which often precedes the fall in 
fertility, has caused a truly exceptional increase in global population.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: In 170 years the population of the world has increased from 1 billion to 4 billion; under the most favorable combinations of fertility and mortal¬ ity of earlier eras the global population would not have doubled in this interval.
text_raw:
In 
170 years the population of the world has increased from 1 billion to 
4 billion; under the most favorable combinations of fertility and mortal¬ 
ity of earlier eras the global population would not have doubled in 
this interval.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The greatest acceleration of growth has been in the re¬ cent experience of the less developed countries, where mortality has dropped very sharply and fertility has not yet fallen.
text_raw:
The greatest acceleration of growth has been in the re¬ 
cent experience of the less developed countries, where mortality has 
dropped very sharply and fertility has not yet fallen.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Mexico’s popula¬ tion has doubled from 30 to 60 million in just 20 years.
text_raw:
Mexico’s popula¬ 
tion has doubled from 30 to 60 million in just 20 years.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The greatest alteration in age distribution resulting from these changes in vital rates is a shift to an older population, caused by the decline in fertility; indeed, the reduction in mortality alone, concentrated as it is at the younger ages, makes a population younger.
text_raw:
The greatest alteration in age distribution resulting from these 
changes in vital rates is a shift to an older population, caused by the 
decline in fertility; indeed, the reduction in mortality alone, concentrated 
as it is at the younger ages, makes a population younger.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The best known set of ideas is the theory of the demographic transition (sometimes called the vital revolution), which finds a persuasive association between the reduction of mortality and fertility and the altered social and economic conditions that are a natural part of the change to modern technology and industrial organi¬ zation.

The best known set of ideas is the theory

and fertility and the altered social and economic conditions that are a 
natural part of the change to modern technology and industrial organi¬ 
zation.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: Many of the ideas that constitute the theory of the demographic transition were developed by European social scientists before World War I and were fully elaborated in Europe and America in the 1930s, 1940s, and 1950s.

chapter_title: Chapter 1: Introduction
text: The demographic transition is invoked in simplified form today to support various positions in politicized debates concern¬ ing the best strategy for moderating very high fertility in the less de¬ veloped countries. “Development is the best contraceptive”—obviously a distillation of the theory—was one of the popular slogans at the World Population Conference in Bucharest in 1974.

chapter_title: Chapter 2: The Evolution of Marital Fertility in
text: Timing of the Decline in Marital Fertility in the Provinces of European Russia In a population as diverse as that of Russia, one would expect the reduction in marital fertility in different provinces to begin at well- separated dates, unless at a particular time overriding, universally ex¬ perienced forces reduced fertility simultaneously in all parts of the coun¬ try.
text_raw:
Timing of the Decline in Marital Fertility in the 
Provinces of European Russia 
In a population as diverse as that of Russia, one would expect the 
reduction in marital fertility in different provinces to begin at well- 
separated dates, unless at a particular time overriding, universally ex¬ 
perienced forces reduced fertility simultaneously in all parts of the coun¬ 
try.

chapter_title: Chapter 2: The Evolution of Marital Fertility in
text: The jagged course of marital fertility in European Russia as a whole since the late nineteenth century (Figure 2.1), with the profound and prolonged depressions of the birth rate from 1915 to 1923, 1929 to 1936, and 1940 to 1946, suggests that there were indeed powerful, universally experienced forces that may have reduced fertility, tem¬ porarily at least, in all segments of the Russian population.
text_raw:
The jagged course of marital fertility in European Russia as a whole 
since the late nineteenth century (Figure 2.1), with the profound and 
prolonged depressions of the birth rate from 1915 to 1923, 1929 to 
1936, and 1940 to 1946, suggests that there were indeed powerful, 
universally experienced forces that may have reduced fertility, tem¬ 
porarily at least, in all segments of the Russian population.

text: MARITAL FERTILITY IN CENTRAL ASIA Variations in Natural Fertility The distinction between natural fertility and controlled fertility is a more realistic and useful way of denoting the contrast between the fertil¬ ity of traditional and modernized societies than the distinction some de¬ mographers have previously used.
text_raw:
MARITAL FERTILITY IN CENTRAL ASIA 
Variations in Natural Fertility 
The distinction between natural fertility and controlled fertility is a 
more realistic and useful way of denoting the contrast between the fertil¬ 
ity of traditional and modernized societies than the distinction some de¬ 
mographers have previously used.

chapter_title: Chapter 3: Marital Fertility in Central Asia
text: The earlier distinction was embodied in the difference between fertility (defined as the rate of childbearing actually achieved in a population) and fecundity (defined as the capac¬ ity to bear children, “capacity” implying the maximum rate that is physiologically possible).
text_raw:
The earlier distinction was embodied 
in the difference between fertility (defined as the rate of childbearing 
actually achieved in a population) and fecundity (defined as the capac¬ 
ity to bear children, “capacity” implying the maximum rate that is 
physiologically possible).

chapter_title: Chapter 3: Marital Fertility in Central Asia
text: It was implied that in traditional populations marital fertility did not differ consequentially from fecundity, and that the fertility of modern populations differs from that of traditional popu¬ lations because it is kept below the level of fecundity by the employ¬ ment of birth-limiting practices.
text_raw:
It was implied that in traditional populations 
marital fertility did not differ consequentially from fecundity, and that 
the fertility of modern populations differs from that of traditional popu¬ 
lations because it is kept below the level of fecundity by the employ¬ 
ment of birth-limiting practices.

chapter_title: Chapter 3: Marital Fertility in Central Asia
text: Henry’s concept of controlled versus natural fertility is based not on a difference in the rate of childbearing, but on a characteristic difference in behavior, that is, not on whether fertility is or is not reduced below the physiologically possible, but on whether practices that affect fertil¬ ity are employed (or modified) only after a certain parity is reached.

chapter_title: Chapter 1 to compare fertility in Russia as a whole at different dates
text: Census survival rates have two convenient virtues: they can be calculated from census data alone, and they incorporate average national recorded attrition for each cohort (a compound of the genuine survival rate of the national cohort, plus biases caused by differences in completeness of coverage of the cohort in the two censuses, and fic¬ titious gains and losses because of age misreporting).
text_raw:
Census survival rates have two convenient virtues: they can 
be calculated from census data alone, and they incorporate average 
national recorded attrition for each cohort (a compound of the genuine 
survival rate of the national cohort, plus biases caused by differences 
in completeness of coverage of the cohort in the two censuses, and fic¬ 
titious gains and losses because of age misreporting).

Notes on the Fertility of the 
Nonmarried Population 
The description and analysis of fertility in Russia has been presented

chapter_title: Chapter 1. Introduction
text: The advantage of these indexes is twofold: although they require no more data than is needed to calculate the general fertility rate (births/ women 15-50), the general marital fertility rate (legitimate births/married women 15-50), and the simple proportion married among women aged 15-50, they have an intuitively appealing interpretation on a scale of zero to one, and they attenuate the influence of the age composition of the women within the childbearing span.
text_raw:
The advantage of these indexes is twofold: although they require no 
more data than is needed to calculate the general fertility rate (births/ women 
15-50), the general marital fertility rate (legitimate births/married women 
15-50), and the simple proportion married among women aged 15-50, they 
have an intuitively appealing interpretation on a scale of zero to one, and they 
attenuate the influence of the age composition of the women within the 
childbearing span.
